# One leak, many published methods

Reference case: a 0.125-in (1/8-in) hole at 100 psig that leaks for 8,760 h/yr. Each method uses its own published defaults. Inputs that the leak does not fix are shared: air temperature 70 F at the compressor inlet and at the leak, motor efficiency 0.90, a single-stage rotary-screw compressor, and 0.18 kW per cfm where a method needs a specific power. Atmospheric pressure is 14.7 psia throughout. Flow is volume of free air at 14.7 psia, as each source defines it: Essentials at compressor-inlet temperature, the Tip Sheet as tabulated, and the Workbook mass flow divided by 0.07494 lbm/ft3 (air at 70 F).

## 1. Methods as published, without a control-mode correction

| Method | Source | Flow (cfm) | Savings (kWh/yr) | Ratio to lowest |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Workbook Fliegner, load factor 0.6 (as in the worked example) | Workbook v2.0, pp. 77-79 | 16.93 | 13,494 | 1.00 |
| Workbook Fliegner, load factor 1.0 | Workbook v2.0, pp. 77-79 | 16.93 | 22,491 | 1.67 |
| Tip Sheet #3 table, sharp x 0.61 | Tip Sheet #3, pp. 1-2 | 15.38 | 24,258 | 1.80 |
| Schmidt & Kissock Moss + rule of thumb | S2004 Eq. 16, PDF p. 8 | 15.84 | 27,523 | 2.04 |
| Essentials v3 Table 6.3 (NBS) | Essentials v3, p. 189 | 19.06 | 29,784 | 2.21 |
| Essentials v3 formula | Essentials v3, pp. 195-198 | 20.85 | 33,079 | 2.45 |
| Tip Sheet #3 table, rounded x 0.97 | Tip Sheet #3, pp. 1-2 | 24.46 | 38,574 | 2.86 |

**Spread: 13,494 to 38,574 kWh/yr, a factor of 2.86.**

Where the spread comes from:

- The low end is the Self-Assessment Workbook with its worked example's average partial-load factor of 0.6. That factor is a plant-specific assumption in the example, not part of Fliegner's formula. Without that row the spread is 22,491 to 38,574 kWh/yr, a factor of 1.72.
- The high end is the Tip Sheet table with the well-rounded orifice factor 0.97. The sharp-orifice factor 0.61 used in the Tip Sheet's own example gives 37 % less for the same hole.
- Flow estimates alone differ by a factor of 1.59 (lowest 15.38, highest 24.46 cfm); the rest comes from how each method converts flow to electricity (specific power, compressor and motor efficiency, isothermal vs. adiabatic compression).

Assumptions behind each row:

- Workbook Fliegner, load factor 0.6 (as in the worked example): k 0.65; T = 70 F; isothermal, eta 0.65; LF 0.6.
- Workbook Fliegner, load factor 1.0: k 0.65; T = 70 F; isothermal, eta 0.65; LF 1.0.
- Tip Sheet #3 table, sharp x 0.61: 0.18 kW/cfm.
- Schmidt & Kissock Moss + rule of thumb: C 0.61; 4.2 cfm/bhp; 0.75 kW/hp; motor 0.90.
- Essentials v3 Table 6.3 (NBS): table value 3.4 kWh per hour of leaking; flow = ft3/yr / 525,600 min.
- Essentials v3 formula: Cd 0.8; Ti = Tl = 70 F; screw Ea 0.82; motor 0.9; 1 stage.
- Tip Sheet #3 table, rounded x 0.97: 0.18 kW/cfm.

For reference only (not a published choice; the Tip Sheet says the table values should be multiplied by 0.97 or 0.61):

- Tip Sheet #3 table, table (no factor): 25.22 cfm, 39,767 kWh/yr.

## 2. With the published control-mode corrections

UMP Chapter 22 multiplies by a trim-compressor control adjustment factor (CCAF, Table 5). Schmidt & Kissock (2004, 2005) multiply the full-load saving by (1 - FP0), the slope of their linear part-load model; FP0 values below are read from their Figure 2 (2005) to the nearest 5 %.

| Method | Flow (cfm) | Savings (kWh/yr) |
|---|---:|---:|
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 1.00 (reciprocating_on_off) | 15.38 | 24,258 |
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 0.97 (screw_variable_speed) | 15.38 | 23,530 |
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 0.74 (reciprocating_load_unload) | 15.38 | 17,951 |
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 0.73 (screw_load_unload_10gal_per_cfm) | 15.38 | 17,708 |
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 0.63 (screw_load_unload_5gal_per_cfm) | 15.38 | 15,282 |
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 0.60 (screw_variable_displacement) | 15.38 | 14,555 |
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 0.53 (screw_load_unload_3gal_per_cfm) | 15.38 | 12,857 |
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 0.43 (screw_load_unload_1gal_per_cfm) | 15.38 | 10,431 |
| UMP Eq. 12, CCAF 0.30 (screw_inlet_modulation) | 15.38 | 7,277 |
| Schmidt & Kissock, (1 - FP0) with FP0 0.70 (inlet_modulation) | 15.84 | 8,257 |
| Schmidt & Kissock, (1 - FP0) with FP0 0.60 (load_unload) | 15.84 | 11,009 |
| Schmidt & Kissock, (1 - FP0) with FP0 0.25 (variable_displacement) | 15.84 | 20,642 |
| Schmidt & Kissock, (1 - FP0) with FP0 0.10 (variable_speed) | 15.84 | 24,771 |
| Schmidt & Kissock, (1 - FP0) with FP0 0.00 (start_stop) | 15.84 | 27,523 |

Across sections 1 and 2 together the estimates run from 7,277 to 38,574 kWh/yr, a factor of 5.30. Control mode alone moves the UMP estimate by a factor of 3.33 (CCAF 1.00 vs 0.30).

## 3. Caveats

- This is a scenario comparison using alternative published assumptions, not a controlled test of the methods: besides the equations, the rows differ in orifice factor, load factor, compressor and control type, and compression model, as listed under each table. Real assessments also differ in the hole size someone estimates by ear, the hours, and the pressure, which this table does not cover.
- The Essentials row depends on the assumed motor efficiency (0.90 here). Its own worked example uses 0.915 but its results table appears to omit the motor efficiency (see worked_examples.md, ESS-2).
- UMP's simplified Equation 12 is valid only for a single trim compressor whose count of running units does not change, in a system that 'is well-controlled and operates predictably' (UMP p. 18); otherwise UMP requires a CFM-bin analysis, which is not implemented. Each CCAF is the slope of the part-load curve between 40 % and 80 % capacity (UMP p. 19).
- All numbers here are computed by `tools/make_docs.py`; `tests/test_behaviour.py` pins the low and high values of section 1.
